summary: Conveys the Internet Activities Board's recommendations for developing network management standards for the TCP/IP environment, in the short and long term. It does not define an official protocol, but reflects IAB policy on further work.

eli5.summary: Before many tools existed for checking on networks, the Internet's planners wrote down what they wanted built and in what order.

questions: what did the iab recommend for network management
how did snmp and cmot start
why was snmp chosen for network management
subtitle: The 1988 policy that chose SNMP for the short term and ISO CMIS/CMIP for the long term.

tldr.problem: By the end of 1987 three network management efforts (HEMS, SGMP and CMIS/CMIP) were far enough along that the community risked ending up with incompatible tools.
tldr.mechanism: An ad hoc review committee met on 29 February 1988 and recommended SNMP as the short-term basis, ISO CMIS/CMIP for the long term, an IETF task force to own SNMP, and a common extended MIB. The IAB endorsed this on 21 March 1988.
tldr.outcome: The memo does not define an official protocol. It records IAB policy and tells the IETF chairman to form working groups for SNMP extensions and for the MIB.

today: RFC 1052 records a policy from April 1988 and is not a protocol specification. The follow-up review is reported in RFC 1109, which says the strict tie between SNMP and CMIP to one MIB had stifled exploration and recommends relaxing it.

sections.title: The IAB Decision
sections.content:
At its videoconference meeting on 21 March 88, the Internet Activities Board (IAB) reviewed the report of the Ad Hoc Network Management Review Committee. It endorsed the recommendations and told the chairman of the Internet Engineering Task Force to carry them out. The IAB thanked the HEMS, SNMP and CMIP/CMIS working groups.

The IETF chairman was to form two new working groups. One would specify the elements of the Management Information Base (MIB). The other would define extensions to the Simple Network Management Protocol for short-term needs of vendors and operators. The longer-term needs were to be met using the ISO CMIS/CMIP framework as a basis. The MIB group's output goes to both the SNMP group and the CMIS/CMIP ("Netman") group so both frameworks monitor compatible items.
sections.eli5: The leaders met by video and said yes to the plan. Then they asked two new teams to get busy: one to improve the simple tool, one to list what the tools should be able to check.

sections.title: The Specific Recommendations
sections.content:
The IAB recommended SNMP as the basis for network management in the short term. Extensions might be needed for extra data types or for functional and performance issues in multi-vendor use. The SNMP working group was urged to keep SNMP simple, to reach consensus quickly and to publish its results in one or more RFCs within the next 90 days. The IETF chairman was to resolve disputes, escalating quickly to the IAB if needed.

The MIB working group was to start equally quickly, using as inputs the MIB definitions in HEMS (RFC 1024), the SNMP IDEA-11 and the CMIS/CMIP IDEAs. The IAB wanted the MIB definitions to serve SNMP in the short term and CMIS/CMIP for TCP/IP in the longer term. The three groups were to coordinate on four goals: rapid convergence for SNMP, rapid convergence for the TCP/IP MIB, a transition path from SNMP to CMIP/CMIS, and an early demonstration of CMIP/CMIS using the TCP/IP MIB.
sections.eli5: The plan: use the simple tool now and keep it simple, write one shared list of things to check, and make sure you can switch to the bigger tool later.

sections.title: The Three Competing Efforts
sections.content:
The committee report explains the choices. HEMS (High-Level Entity Management System) was the most comprehensive, with the most extensive MIB and a query-language approach rather than remote procedure calls. Its team worried that a Remote Operations basis for CMIP may not scale to a very large Internet monitored from a few central sites. Cisco Systems showed vendor interest.

SGMP (Simple Gateway Monitoring Protocol) grew from practical needs at NYSERNET and SURAnet. Its implementations existed in its RFC 1028 form and were in use, and its MIB data types were confined to integers and octet strings. CMIS/CMIP was the ISO initiative: voluminously documented, with almost no implementation yet, its draft proposal out for a second ballot after failing to make Draft International Standard on the first. All three use ASN.1 to represent data structures.
sections.eli5: One tool was the most complete, one was already being used and was simple, and one was a big international design that hardly anyone had built yet.

sections.title: Points of Agreement and Resolution
sections.content:
The committee agreed that Internet development is a joint interest of researchers, vendors and users; that there is still no common understanding of what internetwork management really is; and that the community will learn it by doing it at large scale and with diverse implementations. It also wanted a TCP/IP MIB defined now, a CMIS interface to any surviving scheme as a migration path to ISO, and a seat for the IETF in ANSI, ISO and CCITT.

Craig Partridge offered to drop HEMS in favor of SGMP and CMIS/CMIP, if that led to Internet-wide agreement. The long-term rationale was that GOSIP and ISO would eventually require ISO-based protocols, so the Internet would take the high ground by implementing CMIS/CMIP over TCP/IP and gaining implementation experience. In the short term the Internet needed tools for its rapid growth, and SGMP (or its renamed successor SNMP) was the most advanced and simplest.

The four committee recommendations were: adopt and adapt SNMP now; develop and test CMIS/CMIP for the long term; give SNMP responsibility to an IETF task force; and define an extended MIB as a high priority.
sections.eli5: One team stepped aside so everybody could pull in the same direction. That made it possible to pick a plan in a single day.
